subject: Biology
title: Respiration in Plants
summary: The chapter follows one molecule of glucose from the cytoplasm to the mitochondrion: glycolysis, the two fermentations, oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate, the citric acid cycle, the electron transport system with chemiosmosis, and then the bookkeeping of ATP, the amphibolic nature of the pathway and the respiratory quotient. It is the base for Class 12 boards and NEET; the exam wants exact enzyme names, exact sites, exact counts of ATP, NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>, and the three NCERT figures drawn from memory.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Respiration in Plants sits in Unit IV, Plant Physiology, which carries about 12 marks shared with Photosynthesis in Higher Plants and Plant Growth and Development. In a typical school final this chapter alone brings 5 to 8 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ on the site of a step, the enzyme of a step, RQ of a substrate, or the ATP yield of NADH), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on fermentation versus aerobic respiration, the assumptions of the balance sheet, RQ or the amphibolic pathway, and often a 5-mark question on glycolysis, the citric acid cycle or the ETS with a labelled diagram. In NEET it is a steady two-question chapter, with the questions lifted almost word for word from NCERT sentences and figures.

question_types.note: Site of glycolysis (cytoplasm) and of the citric acid cycle (mitochondrial matrix) and of the ETS (inner mitochondrial membrane); the enzyme of a named step (hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, enolase, pyruvate kinase, pyruvic acid decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase, lactate dehydrogenase, pyruvic dehydrogenase, citrate synthase, succinate dehydrogenase, cytochrome c oxidase); the step of GTP formation (succinyl-CoA to succinic acid); the number of NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> per turn of the cycle; ATP from one NADH (3) and one FADH<sub>2</sub> (2); the final electron acceptor (oxygen); the RQ of carbohydrates (1), fats (about 0.7) and proteins (about 0.9); the alcohol concentration at which yeast dies (about 13 per cent); the molecule common to breakdown of fats, carbohydrates and proteins (acetyl CoA); who discovered the cycle (Hans Krebs, 1937) and the pathway (Embden, Meyerhof, Parnas).

Fermentation yields little energy because glucose is only partly oxidised; oxygen does not take part in the Krebs cycle directly yet aerobic respiration needs it because oxygen is the final hydrogen acceptor; RQ of fats is below one; the respiratory pathway is amphibolic; glycolysis needs no oxygen; ATP synthase is complex V; plants do not need specialised breathing organs; the net gain is 36 not 38 ATP.

Define RQ and give its value for fats; two differences between fermentation and aerobic respiration; what is oxidative decarboxylation; what is substrate-level phosphorylation with one example from glycolysis and one from the citric acid cycle; roles of F<sub>0</sub> and F<sub>1</sub>; why is the pathway called amphibolic; what are respiratory substrates; name the enzyme and coenzyme of the link reaction; why do plants not need breathing organs (two reasons); the fate of pyruvate under three conditions.

Explain fermentation in yeast with the equation and the two enzymes; explain oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis; the four assumptions of the respiratory balance sheet; distinguish glycolysis from the citric acid cycle (three points); significance of step-wise release of energy; RQ calculation for tripalmitin; the overall reaction of the citric acid cycle; the three fates of pyruvic acid with the enzyme of each.

Describe glycolysis with the schematic and mark the two ATP-consuming and two ATP-forming steps; describe the citric acid cycle with the schematic and the tally per acetyl CoA; describe the ETS with the labelled diagram of the five complexes and the role of oxygen; the NCERT exercise 12.1 and 12.7 sets of differences (respiration versus combustion, glycolysis versus Krebs cycle, aerobic respiration versus fermentation, aerobic versus anaerobic respiration, glycolysis versus citric acid cycle); prepare the balance sheet and show how 36 ATP arise.

A passage on a germinating-seed respirometer experiment giving different RQ values, on a brewery or bread dough where yeast ferments, on an athlete's muscle cramp, or on a mitochondrion drawing with sites to identify, followed by four sub-questions.

hot_topics: Glycolysis: the ten steps, the two ATP-using and two ATP-making steps, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH (Fig. 12.1)
Fermentation: alcoholic and lactic acid, the enzymes, why less than 7 per cent of energy is released, yeast dying at about 13 per cent alcohol (Fig. 12.2)
Citric acid (Krebs, TCA) cycle: the schematic, the GTP step, 3 NADH + 1 FADH<sub>2</sub> per turn and the overall equation (Fig. 12.3)
Electron transport system: complexes I to V, ubiquinone and cytochrome c as mobile carriers, oxygen as the final acceptor (Fig. 12.4)
Oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis: F<sub>0</sub>, F<sub>1</sub>, 2H<sup>+</sup> per ATP, 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>
Respiratory balance sheet: the four assumptions and the net 36 ATP per glucose
Amphibolic pathway: where fats, glycerol and amino acids enter, and what is withdrawn for synthesis (Fig. 12.5)
Respiratory quotient: definition, RQ of carbohydrates, fats (tripalmitin 0.7) and proteins

sections.heading: Introduction: why cells respire and what they respire
sections.body:
Every living cell needs energy to grow, divide, transport substances across membranes and make its own molecules. That energy comes from the oxidation of macromolecules in the cell, and the process is called cellular respiration. The compounds that are oxidised are the respiratory substrates: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and organic acids. Glucose is the most common respiratory substrate, and the exam expects you to say so in those exact words. In plants, sucrose made in the leaf is first split by the enzyme invertase into glucose and fructose, and both enter the pathway.

Write the overall equation once and remember its shape:

C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy

Two things about this equation matter for marks. First, it is a summary, not a single step. Glucose is broken down in a long series of small enzyme-catalysed steps, each releasing a little energy. NCERT stresses that the energy is not released free into the cell in a single step; it is released in a series of slow, enzyme-controlled steps and trapped as ATP. Combustion releases it all at once as heat and light, respiration does not. The step-wise release is what allows some of the energy to be trapped rather than lost as heat. Second, the energy that is released is not used directly. It is used to make ATP (adenosine triphosphate) from ADP and inorganic phosphate, and ATP is broken down wherever and whenever the cell needs energy. That is why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.

The chapter therefore has one story: how does glucose become CO2 and water, and how many ATP does the cell get on the way? Keep the sites in mind from the start. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm of every cell, whether it has oxygen or not; everything after pyruvic acid that needs oxygen happens inside the mitochondrion, the link reaction and the citric acid cycle in the matrix and the electron transport system on the inner membrane. Almost every 1-mark question in this chapter is a question about a site or an enzyme, so learn the place of each step as you learn the step.

where: glucose, the most common respiratory substrate
released in many small steps and trapped as ATP, not in a single burst as in combustion

sections.tip: If asked why respiration is compared to combustion, name the likeness (both oxidise glucose to CO<sub>2</sub> and water with release of energy) and the two differences the examiner wants: respiration is enzyme-controlled and step-wise at body temperature, combustion is uncontrolled and releases all the energy as heat and light in one step.

sections.heading: 12.1 Do Plants Breathe?
sections.body:
Animals breathe: they have lungs or gills that move gases in and out. Plants do not. Yet plants need O2 for respiration and give out CO2, so gas exchange must happen somehow. The NCERT answer is that plants have no specialised organs for gas exchange, and use stomata on leaves and young stems and lenticels on woody stems and roots. Each plant part takes care of its own gas exchange needs; there is no transport of gases from one organ to another, and only a very small quantity of gas is carried by the transport system.

Why can plants get away without lungs? The chapter gives reasons you should be able to list as a 2-mark or 3-mark answer:

  • Each part of the plant takes care of its own gas-exchange needs, so there is no need to move gases around the body.
  • Plants do not present great demands for gas exchange. Roots, stems and leaves respire at rates far lower than animals do.
  • During photosynthesis, O2 is released within the cell, so the leaf cells are supplied with oxygen while they are photosynthesising.
  • Cells that are living are located close to the surface of the plant. In stems the living cells are arranged in thin layers under the bark, and they have openings (lenticels); in leaves most cells are near the surface anyway.
  • A large part of the bulky plant body is made of dead cells (wood) or loosely packed parenchyma with large intercellular spaces, so gases diffuse easily through the plant body. The distance a gas has to diffuse is never very large.

The examiner also likes the distinction between breathing and respiration. Breathing is the physical process of taking in O2 and giving out CO2, whatever organ does it. Respiration is the chemical process inside the cell where the substrate is oxidised and energy is trapped as ATP. Plants respire in every living cell, but they do not breathe in the animal sense; they simply let gases diffuse in and out through stomata and lenticels.

One more fact that gets asked: because glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen, all living cells, plant or animal, aerobic or anaerobic, carry out glycolysis. Only the fate of pyruvic acid depends on whether oxygen is available.
sections.tip: Do not answer 'plants breathe through stomata' as if it were the whole answer. Add that each part meets its own need, that the demand is low, and that living cells lie close to the surface with air spaces between them.

sections.heading: 12.2 Glycolysis
sections.body:
The name means splitting of sugar (glycos, sugar; lysis, splitting). The scheme was worked out by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas, so it is also called the EMP pathway. It is the partial oxidation of one molecule of glucose (6C) to two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C). It takes place in the cytoplasm, needs no oxygen and occurs in all living organisms. In anaerobic organisms it is the only process in respiration.

NCERT describes ten steps, each with an enzyme, and the marking scheme rewards the schematic in Fig. 12.1 drawn in order. Learn it as a story in three parts.

Part 1, spend two ATP to activate the sugar. Glucose is phosphorylated by hexokinase to glucose-6-phosphate (one ATP used). This isomerises to fructose-6-phosphate. Phosphofructokinase then adds a second phosphate using a second ATP to give fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. These are the only two ATP-consuming steps; NCERT names them as the conversion of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate and of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.

Part 2, split the sugar. Aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two 3-carbon molecules, dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL). DHAP is isomerised to PGAL, so from here on everything happens twice per glucose.

Part 3, oxidise and harvest. PGAL is oxidised and phosphorylated to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA); the two hydrogen atoms (redox equivalents) removed from PGAL are transferred to NAD+, forming NADH + H+. BPGA gives up one phosphate to ADP and becomes 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA); this is an ATP-forming step. 3-PGA rearranges to 2-phosphoglycerate, which loses a water molecule (enolase) to become phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP). PEP transfers its phosphate to ADP (pyruvate kinase) to give pyruvic acid and the second ATP. Both ATP-forming steps are examples of substrate-level phosphorylation: the phosphate comes straight from a substrate molecule, not from an electron transport chain.

Now count. Two ATP are used in part 1. Four ATP are made in part 3 (two steps, each occurring twice). Net gain: 2 ATP and 2 NADH + H+ per glucose, plus two pyruvic acid. The exam asks this count in every form.

Pyruvic acid is the key product of glycolysis, and its fate depends on the cell and on oxygen. NCERT names three major ways: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration. Fermentation happens under anaerobic conditions in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes; aerobic respiration needs oxygen and, in eukaryotes, mitochondria.

where: net: 4 formed by substrate-level phosphorylation minus 2 used in the first phase

formulas.expr: ATP used: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase); fructose-6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase)

sections.tip: The most common 1-mark trap: the reduced coenzyme in glycolysis is NADH + H<sup>+</sup> (from NAD<sup>+</sup>), never NADPH, which belongs to photosynthesis. And in a plant, sucrose is split by invertase before glycolysis, so both glucose and fructose enter the pathway.

sections.heading: 12.3 Fermentation
sections.body:
When there is no oxygen, pyruvic acid cannot enter the mitochondrion for complete oxidation. The cell then does the minimum needed to keep glycolysis running: it reoxidises the NADH + H+ made in glycolysis back to NAD+, because without NAD+ the PGAL step would stop and no more ATP could be made. This incomplete oxidation of glucose is called fermentation, and NCERT describes two kinds.

Alcoholic fermentation in yeast. Pyruvic acid is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde by pyruvic acid decarboxylase, releasing CO2. Then acetaldehyde is reduced by alcohol dehydrogenase to ethanol, and NADH + H+ is oxidised to NAD+ in the process. Overall, one glucose gives two ethanol and two CO2. This is the reaction that makes bread rise and makes beer and wine.

Lactic acid fermentation in some bacteria and in animal muscle during heavy exercise, when oxygen is inadequate. Pyruvic acid is reduced directly to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase, again oxidising NADH + H+ to NAD+. No CO2 is released. In both cases the reducing agent is NADH + H+, which is reoxidised to NAD+; this recycling is the point of fermentation.

Three exam facts about the yield:

  • In both fermentations very little energy is released: less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose is released, and not all of it is trapped as high-energy bonds of ATP. The net gain is only the 2 ATP of glycolysis.
  • Fermentation is a partial breakdown of glucose; aerobic respiration degrades glucose completely to CO2 and H2O.
  • The products are toxic. Yeasts poison themselves to death when the concentration of alcohol reaches about 13 per cent, which is why naturally fermented beverages are not stronger than that; spirits are made by distillation.

NCERT's Fig. 12.2 summarises the major pathways of anaerobic respiration: glucose → pyruvic acid, and then three arrows, to lactic acid (lactate dehydrogenase), to ethanol + CO2 (pyruvic acid decarboxylase then alcohol dehydrogenase) and to acetyl CoA + CO2 for aerobic respiration. Draw it for any question on the fate of pyruvic acid.

NCERT treats fermentation and anaerobic respiration together, and the comparison the examiner cares about is with aerobic respiration: no oxygen needed, no mitochondrion, no complete oxidation, no ETS, NADH oxidised by the organic acceptor (pyruvate or acetaldehyde) rather than by oxygen, and only 2 ATP.

formulas.expr: Pyruvic acid → (pyruvic acid decarboxylase, CO<sub>2</sub> released) Acetaldehyde → (alcohol dehydrogenase, NADH + H<sup>+</sup> → NAD<sup>+</sup>) Ethanol
Pyruvic acid + NADH + H<sup>+</sup> → (lactate dehydrogenase) Lactic acid + NAD<sup>+</sup>
where: some bacteria and animal muscle short of oxygen; no CO<sub>2</sub> released

sections.tip: Write the enzyme names in full: pyruvic acid decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase, lactate dehydrogenase. A 2-mark question on fermentation without the enzymes loses a mark.

sections.heading: 12.4 Aerobic Respiration: entry into the mitochondrion and the link reaction
sections.body:
Aerobic respiration is the process that leads to the complete oxidation of organic substances in the presence of oxygen, releasing CO2, water and a large amount of energy. In eukaryotes it happens in the mitochondria, so the pyruvic acid made in the cytoplasm must first be transported into the mitochondrial matrix. The chapter describes two crucial events that follow: the complete oxidation of pyruvate by step-wise removal of all the hydrogen atoms, leaving three molecules of CO2; and the passing of those electrons to molecular O2 with simultaneous synthesis of ATP. The first happens in the matrix, the second on the inner membrane.

The link reaction (oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate). Inside the matrix, pyruvic acid (3C) undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by a complex set of reactions catalysed by pyruvic dehydrogenase. The reaction needs the participation of several coenzymes, including NAD+ and Coenzyme A. One carbon leaves as CO2, the remaining two-carbon acetyl group is attached to CoA to give acetyl CoA, and NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+.

Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD+ → Acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+ (pyruvic dehydrogenase, Mg2+)

Since one glucose gives two pyruvic acid, this step produces 2 NADH + H+ and 2 CO2 per glucose. Call it oxidative decarboxylation in the exam: oxidative because NAD+ is reduced (pyruvate is oxidised), decarboxylation because CO2 is removed. Acetyl CoA then enters the cyclic pathway, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, described next.

Why is acetyl CoA important beyond this chapter? It is the molecule where the breakdown of fats, carbohydrates and proteins meet: fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, several amino acids are converted to it, and glucose reaches it through pyruvate. NEET has asked exactly this twice: the biomolecule common to respiration-mediated breakdown of fats, carbohydrates and proteins is acetyl CoA, not pyruvic acid.

Keep the sites straight for the whole of aerobic respiration: glycolysis in the cytoplasm; link reaction and citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; ETS and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Draw a mitochondrion once with these three labels and the 1-mark site questions stop being a risk.

formulas.expr: Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD<sup>+</sup> → Acetyl CoA + CO<sub>2</sub> + NADH + H<sup>+</sup>
where: pyruvic dehydrogenase, in the mitochondrial matrix, with Mg<sup>2+</sup>

sections.tip: Pyruvate does not enter the Krebs cycle. Acetyl CoA does. A 1-mark MCQ on what condenses with oxaloacetic acid is answered 'acetyl CoA', and NEET 2017 marked 'cycle starts with condensation of the acetyl group with pyruvic acid' as the incorrect statement.

sections.heading: 12.4.1 Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle (Citric Acid Cycle, Krebs Cycle)
sections.body:
The cycle was first elucidated by Hans Krebs in 1937, hence Krebs cycle. Because the first product, citric acid, has three carboxyl groups it is also the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle or citric acid cycle. It runs in the mitochondrial matrix.

Entry. Acetyl CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetic acid (OAA, 4C) and water to give citric acid (6C), catalysed by citrate synthase; a molecule of CoA is released and goes back to pick up another acetyl group. Citrate is then isomerised to isocitrate.

Two decarboxylations. Isocitrate loses one CO2 and is oxidised (NAD+ → NADH + H+) to α-ketoglutaric acid (5C). α-Ketoglutaric acid loses a second CO2, is oxidised again (a second NADH + H+) and joins CoA to become succinyl-CoA (4C). These are the two CO2 molecules of one turn; together with the CO2 of the link reaction they account for the three carbons of one pyruvate.

The GTP step. Succinyl-CoA is converted to succinic acid and CoA is released; the energy of the thioester bond is used to make a molecule of GTP from GDP and Pi. This is a substrate-level phosphorylation, the only one in the cycle. In a coupled reaction GTP is converted to GDP with simultaneous synthesis of ATP from ADP, so it is counted as one ATP.

Regeneration of OAA. Succinic acid is oxidised to fumaric acid by succinate dehydrogenase; here the acceptor is FAD, which becomes FADH2 (the only FADH2 of the cycle). Fumaric acid takes up water to give malic acid, and malic acid is oxidised (third NADH + H+) to oxaloacetic acid, which is ready to accept the next acetyl CoA. The continued oxidation of acetyl CoA therefore needs the continued replenishment of OAA and the regeneration of NAD+ and FAD.

Tally per turn (per acetyl CoA): 2 CO2, 3 NADH + H+, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (= 1 ATP). Per glucose the cycle turns twice, so 4 CO2, 6 NADH + H+, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP. NCERT gives the summary equation for one pyruvic acid, which includes the link reaction:

Pyruvic acid + 4NAD+ + FAD + 2H2O + ADP + Pi → 3CO2 + 4NADH + 4H+ + FADH2 + ATP

Note what the cycle does not do: no oxygen is used directly, and only one ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation. Its real output is reduced coenzymes, NADH + H+ and FADH2, whose oxidation in the ETS produces most of the cell's ATP. Also note that the cycle needs oxygen indirectly, because the NAD+ and FAD it requires are regenerated only when the ETS passes their electrons to oxygen.

formulas.expr: Pyruvic acid + 4NAD<sup>+</sup> + FAD + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + ADP + Pi → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4NADH + 4H<sup>+</sup> + FADH<sub>2</sub> + ATP
where: 1 from the link reaction + 3 from the cycle (isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, malate steps)
from succinic acid → fumaric acid (succinate dehydrogenase)
via GTP at succinyl-CoA → succinic acid

formulas.expr: Acetyl CoA (2C) + OAA (4C) + H<sub>2</sub>O → Citric acid (6C) + CoA (citrate synthase)
where: citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (5C) → succinyl-CoA (4C) → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate

sections.tip: NCERT prints the oxidised flavin as FAD<sup>+</sup> in the equation; if you copy it that way you will not be penalised, but FAD/FADH<sub>2</sub> is the correct pair. What loses marks is writing that ATP is formed at the succinate step or that FADH<sub>2</sub> is formed at the malate step; keep GTP at succinyl-CoA → succinate and FADH<sub>2</sub> at succinate → fumarate.

sections.heading: 12.4.2 Electron Transport System (ETS) and Oxidative Phosphorylation
sections.body:
So far the energy of glucose has been parked in NADH + H+ and FADH2. The electron transport system on the inner mitochondrial membrane releases and uses that energy: electrons are passed from one carrier to another and finally to oxygen, and the energy released on the way is used to make ATP. This is the metabolic pathway through which the electron passes from one carrier to another.

The carriers, in order (NCERT Fig. 12.4).

  • Complex I, NADH dehydrogenase. Electrons from NADH produced in the mitochondrial matrix during the citric acid cycle are oxidised here and passed to ubiquinone (UQ), a mobile carrier within the inner membrane.
  • Complex II, succinate dehydrogenase. Ubiquinone also receives reducing equivalents from FADH2, which is generated during the oxidation of succinate in the citric acid cycle. This is why the FADH2 electrons skip complex I and yield fewer ATP.
  • Complex III, cytochrome bc1 complex. Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) is oxidised and the electrons are transferred to cytochrome c.
  • Cytochrome c is a small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane; it is a mobile carrier of electrons between complex III and complex IV.
  • Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase. Contains cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres. It hands the electrons to molecular oxygen, the final acceptor, which is reduced to water.

Where the ATP comes from. When the electrons pass through the chain, they are coupled to ATP synthase (complex V) for the production of ATP from ADP and Pi. The number of ATP depends on the electron donor: oxidation of one NADH gives 3 ATP, of one FADH2 gives 2 ATP.

Chemiosmosis and ATP synthase. As electrons move through the complexes, protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient across the inner membrane. ATP synthase has two parts. F1 is the headpiece, a peripheral membrane protein complex that contains the site for synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi. F0 is an integral membrane protein complex that forms the channel through which protons cross the inner membrane. The passage of protons through the channel is coupled to the catalytic site of F1. NCERT's number: for each ATP produced, 2H+ pass through F0 from the intermembrane space to the matrix down the electrochemical proton gradient. Because the ATP is made by oxidation of the coenzymes with oxygen as the acceptor, the process is called oxidative phosphorylation, as opposed to photophosphorylation in the chloroplast where the energy comes from light.

Role of oxygen. Oxygen is used only at the end of the pathway, yet it is essential for the whole of aerobic respiration. NCERT puts it simply: the role of oxygen is limited to the terminal stage, but its presence is vital because it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system. Oxygen acts as the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor. Without it the carriers stay reduced, NAD+ and FAD are not regenerated, and the citric acid cycle stops.

formulas.expr: NADH → Complex I → UQ → Complex III → Cyt c → Complex IV → ½O<sub>2</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>O (3 ATP);   FADH<sub>2</sub> → Complex II → UQ → Complex III → Cyt c → Complex IV → ½O<sub>2</sub> (2 ATP)
where: ubiquinone, mobile within the inner membrane
cytochrome c, mobile on the outer surface of the inner membrane
ATP synthase: F<sub>0</sub> channel + F<sub>1</sub> catalytic head; 2H<sup>+</sup> per ATP

sections.tip: Two separate facts get merged wrongly: the final electron acceptor is oxygen (not cytochrome c oxidase, which is the enzyme that delivers to oxygen), and ATP synthase does not carry electrons at all. Draw the five complexes left to right with UQ and cyt c between them and label F<sub>0</sub> in the membrane, F<sub>1</sub> projecting into the matrix.

sections.heading: 12.5 The Respiratory Balance Sheet
sections.body:
The balance sheet is the exam's favourite arithmetic. NCERT is honest that the calculation is theoretical and rests on four assumptions that are not really valid in a living system; the assumptions themselves are a 2-mark or 3-mark question (NCERT exercise 12.8).

  1. There is a sequential, orderly pathway functioning, with one substrate forming the next and with glycolysis, TCA cycle and ETS following one after another.
  2. The NADH synthesised in glycolysis is transferred into the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation.
  3. None of the intermediates in the pathway are utilised to synthesise any other compound.
  4. Only glucose is being respired; no other alternative substrates enter the pathway at any of the intermediary stages.

In reality all pathways work simultaneously, substrates enter and leave at many points, ATP is used as and when needed, and enzyme rates change. Still, the calculation gives a useful figure.

The tally per glucose.

  • Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 2 ATP (substrate level) + 2 NADH + H+.
  • Link reaction (matrix): 2 NADH + H+.
  • Citric acid cycle, two turns (matrix): 2 ATP via GTP + 6 NADH + H+ + 2 FADH2.
  • Totals of reduced coenzymes: 10 NADH + H+ and 2 FADH2.
  • ETS (inner membrane): 10 × 3 = 30 ATP from NADH, 2 × 2 = 4 ATP from FADH2.

Adding: 2 + 2 + 30 + 4 = 38 ATP if every NADH gives three ATP. NCERT states that there can be a net gain of 36 ATP molecules during aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose; the difference is that the 2 NADH made in the cytoplasm during glycolysis have to be moved into the mitochondrion, and the transport costs the equivalent of 2 ATP. Give 36 as the NCERT answer and explain the 38 when asked to show working.

Fermentation versus aerobic respiration, the comparison NCERT draws at the end of this section, is asked every year:

  • Fermentation is a partial breakdown of glucose; in aerobic respiration glucose is completely degraded to CO2 and H2O.
  • Fermentation gives a net gain of only 2 ATP per glucose; aerobic respiration gives many more, 36.
  • In fermentation NADH is oxidised to NAD+ rather slowly, by pyruvate or acetaldehyde; in aerobic respiration it is oxidised vigorously by the ETS with oxygen as the acceptor.

formulas.expr: ATP per glucose = 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (TCA via GTP) + 10 NADH × 3 + 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> × 2 = 38; net 36 after 2 ATP spent moving cytoplasmic NADH into the mitochondrion
where: 2 glycolysis + 2 link reaction + 6 citric acid cycle
one per turn of the cycle, at succinate → fumarate

sections.tip: If the question asks for the number NCERT gives, write 36 and add one line on the 2 ATP transport cost. If it asks you to 'calculate assuming 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>', show 38 and then state the net 36. Never write 36 without being able to show where it came from.

sections.heading: 12.6 Amphibolic Pathway
sections.body:
Glucose is the favoured substrate, but cells respire other things too, and they enter the same pathway at different points. NCERT's Fig. 12.5 (interrelationship among metabolic pathways) is the picture to remember.

  • Fats are first broken down into glycerol and fatty acids. Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle. Glycerol enters glycolysis as PGAL (3-phosphoglyceraldehyde).
  • Proteins are degraded by proteases to amino acids, and the amino acids, after deamination, enter at different points: some as pyruvate, some as acetyl CoA, some as intermediates of the citric acid cycle such as α-ketoglutaric acid or oxaloacetic acid.
  • Carbohydrates other than glucose (starch, sucrose, fructose) are converted to glucose or its phosphates and enter glycolysis.

So far this is catabolism, the breakdown of molecules. The important point is that the same pathway also runs the other way. When the organism needs to synthesise fatty acids, acetyl CoA is withdrawn from the respiratory pathway. Many amino acids are made from intermediates of the citric acid cycle. Glycerol for fat synthesis comes from PGAL. That is anabolism, biosynthesis, using respiratory intermediates as starting material.

Since the respiratory pathway is involved in both breakdown and synthesis, it is better to call it an amphibolic pathway rather than a purely catabolic one. That single sentence, with two examples on each side, is the model 2-mark answer for NCERT exercise 12.9. For a 3-mark version, add that this is why a cell cannot stop respiring even when it has plenty of ATP: the intermediates are needed as building blocks, which is also assumption 3 of the balance sheet being violated in real life.

Two definitions to keep separate. Catabolic pathways break large molecules down and release energy; anabolic pathways build molecules and use energy; amphibolic pathways do both. Respiration is often described as catabolic in short answers (and 'catabolic' is the accepted answer to 'is respiration catabolic or anabolic'), but when the question uses the word amphibolic, the examiner wants the dual role explained.

formulas.expr: Fats → glycerol (→ PGAL, glycolysis) + fatty acids (→ acetyl CoA, TCA);   Proteins → amino acids (→ pyruvate / acetyl CoA / α-ketoglutarate / OAA)
where: acetyl CoA → fatty acids; TCA intermediates → amino acids; PGAL → glycerol

sections.tip: Give both directions with a named molecule each: 'fatty acids broken to acetyl CoA (catabolic); acetyl CoA withdrawn for fatty-acid synthesis (anabolic).' A definition alone earns half.

sections.heading: 12.7 Respiratory Quotient
sections.body:
During aerobic respiration O2 is consumed and CO2 is released. The ratio of the volume of CO2 evolved to the volume of O2 consumed in respiration is called the respiratory quotient (RQ) or respiratory ratio.

RQ = volume of CO2 evolved / volume of O2 consumed

The value depends on the respiratory substrate, and the exam asks the three standard cases.

Carbohydrates, RQ = 1. From the overall equation, 6 O2 consumed and 6 CO2 evolved, so RQ = 6CO2/6O2 = 1.0.

Fats, RQ less than 1. Fats contain very little oxygen relative to carbon and hydrogen, so they need extra O2 to oxidise their hydrogen, and less CO2 comes out per O2 used. NCERT's example is tripalmitin:

2(C51H98O6) + 145O2 → 102CO2 + 98H2O + energy

RQ = 102CO2/145O2 = 0.7. Check the arithmetic once so you can reproduce it: 102 ÷ 145 = 0.703, written as 0.7.

Proteins, RQ about 0.9. NCERT states that when proteins are the respiratory substrate the ratio would be about 0.9.

Two qualifications the examiner may probe. First, in living organisms pure substrates are rarely used alone; the RQ of a tissue reflects a mixture. Second, RQ is defined for aerobic respiration; in anaerobic conditions (fermentation) CO2 is released without O2 being consumed, so the ratio is not meaningful (it would tend to infinity). Case-based questions build on this with a germinating-seed experiment: starchy seeds such as wheat give RQ close to 1, oily seeds such as castor give a value below 1, and a seed sealed without oxygen releases CO2 without consuming O2.

Why does RQ matter beyond the number? Measuring it tells a physiologist which substrate a tissue is burning, which is useful in studying germinating seeds, ripening fruit or a stressed plant. But for the exam the definition, the formula, the three values and the tripalmitin calculation are the four things to have ready.

formulas.expr: RQ = volume of CO<sub>2</sub> evolved / volume of O<sub>2</sub> consumed

where: tripalmitin, NCERT's example of a fat

sections.tip: RQ is a ratio of volumes, so write 'volume of CO<sub>2</sub> evolved' and 'volume of O<sub>2</sub> consumed', not 'amount' or 'moles'. And the order matters: CO<sub>2</sub> on top.

key_terms.definition: The enzyme-controlled, step-wise oxidation of respiratory substrates such as glucose within the cell, releasing energy that is trapped as ATP, with CO<sub>2</sub> and water as products under aerobic conditions.
A compound oxidised in respiration to release energy: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and organic acids. Glucose is the most common respiratory substrate.
Adenosine triphosphate, the molecule in which the energy released in respiration is stored and from which it is withdrawn whenever the cell needs it.

Partial oxidation of one glucose (6C) to two pyruvic acid (3C) in the cytoplasm through ten enzyme steps, without oxygen, giving a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH + H<sup>+</sup>; named after Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas.

Formation of ATP (or GTP) by direct transfer of a phosphate from a substrate molecule to ADP (or GDP), as at BPGA → 3-PGA and PEP → pyruvate in glycolysis and succinyl-CoA → succinate in the citric acid cycle.

Incomplete oxidation of glucose under anaerobic conditions in which pyruvic acid is reduced to ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub> (yeast) or to lactic acid (some bacteria, muscle), regenerating NAD<sup>+</sup> so that glycolysis continues; net 2 ATP, less than 7 per cent of the energy of glucose released.
The complete oxidation of organic substrates in the presence of oxygen to CO<sub>2</sub> and water with release of a large amount of energy; in eukaryotes it occurs in the mitochondria.

Removal of CO<sub>2</sub> from a compound with simultaneous oxidation; pyruvic acid is converted to acetyl CoA, CO<sub>2</sub> and NADH + H<sup>+</sup> this way by pyruvic dehydrogenase in the mitochondrial matrix.

The two-carbon acetyl group attached to coenzyme A, formed from pyruvate, fatty acids and some amino acids; it condenses with oxaloacetic acid to enter the citric acid cycle and is the common meeting point for breakdown of fats, carbohydrates and proteins.

key_terms.term: Tricarboxylic acid cycle (Krebs cycle, citric acid cycle)
key_terms.definition: The cyclic pathway in the mitochondrial matrix, elucidated by Hans Krebs in 1937, in which acetyl CoA is oxidised to two CO<sub>2</sub> with formation of 3 NADH + H<sup>+</sup>, 1 FADH<sub>2</sub> and 1 GTP per turn, regenerating oxaloacetic acid.

The chain of carriers (complexes I to IV, ubiquinone, cytochrome c) on the inner mitochondrial membrane through which electrons from NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> pass to oxygen, releasing energy used to make ATP.

Synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi by ATP synthase using the energy of a proton gradient created when electrons pass along the ETS to oxygen; distinguished from photophosphorylation, where light supplies the energy.

The mechanism of oxidative phosphorylation in which protons pumped into the intermembrane space flow back into the matrix through the F<sub>0</sub> channel of ATP synthase, driving ATP formation at the F<sub>1</sub> head; 2H<sup>+</sup> per ATP.
The enzyme of the inner mitochondrial membrane with an F<sub>1</sub> peripheral headpiece containing the ATP-synthesising site and an F<sub>0</sub> integral membrane part forming the proton channel.
A mobile electron carrier within the inner mitochondrial membrane that receives electrons from complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) and passes them to complex III.
A small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane that carries electrons from complex III (cytochrome bc<sub>1</sub>) to complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase).
The last complex of the ETS, containing cytochromes a and a<sub>3</sub> and two copper centres, which transfers electrons to molecular oxygen, the final acceptor, reducing it to water.

The theoretical count of ATP formed per glucose in aerobic respiration, 36 net according to NCERT (38 before the cost of moving cytoplasmic NADH into the mitochondrion), made under four simplifying assumptions.

A pathway that serves both catabolism and anabolism; respiration breaks down fats, proteins and carbohydrates through its intermediates and also supplies acetyl CoA, PGAL and citric-acid-cycle intermediates for synthesis of fatty acids, glycerol and amino acids.
The ratio of the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> evolved to the volume of O<sub>2</sub> consumed in respiration; 1 for carbohydrates, about 0.7 for fats and about 0.9 for proteins.
Openings in the bark of woody stems and roots through which gases diffuse in and out; with stomata they meet the gas-exchange needs of a plant, which has no specialised breathing organs.

formula_sheet.name: Overall aerobic respiration
formula_sheet.note: A summary of many enzyme steps; the step-wise release is what separates respiration from combustion.

formula_sheet.name: Sites
formula_sheet.expr: Glycolysis: cytoplasm. Link reaction and citric acid cycle: mitochondrial matrix. ETS and oxidative phosphorylation: inner mitochondrial membrane. Fermentation: cytoplasm.
formula_sheet.note: The single most common 1-mark question in the chapter.

formula_sheet.name: Glycolysis net
formula_sheet.expr: Glucose → 2 pyruvic acid + 2 ATP (net) + 2 NADH + H<sup>+</sup>; ATP used at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase steps; ATP made at BPGA → 3-PGA and PEP → pyruvate
formula_sheet.note: Gross 4 ATP, minus 2 spent. Aldolase splits F-1,6-BP into DHAP and PGAL; enolase makes PEP; pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate.

formula_sheet.name: Three fates of pyruvic acid
formula_sheet.expr: Lactic acid (lactate dehydrogenase, bacteria and muscle); ethanol + CO<sub>2</sub> (pyruvic acid decarboxylase then alcohol dehydrogenase, yeast); acetyl CoA + CO<sub>2</sub> (pyruvic dehydrogenase, aerobic, matrix)
formula_sheet.note: NCERT Fig. 12.2. Fermentation releases under 7 per cent of the energy in glucose; yeast dies at about 13 per cent alcohol.

formula_sheet.name: Link reaction
formula_sheet.expr: Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD<sup>+</sup> → Acetyl CoA + CO<sub>2</sub> + NADH + H<sup>+</sup>
formula_sheet.note: Pyruvic dehydrogenase with Mg<sup>2+</sup>; coenzymes NAD<sup>+</sup> and CoA; twice per glucose.

formula_sheet.name: Citric acid cycle per turn
formula_sheet.expr: Acetyl CoA + OAA → citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA → succinate → fumarate → malate → OAA; yields 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, 3 NADH + H<sup>+</sup>, 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>, 1 GTP
formula_sheet.note: Citrate synthase starts it; GTP at succinyl-CoA → succinate; FADH<sub>2</sub> at succinate → fumarate (succinate dehydrogenase); NADH at isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate and malate steps. Hans Krebs, 1937.

formula_sheet.name: NCERT summary per pyruvate
formula_sheet.expr: Pyruvic acid + 4NAD<sup>+</sup> + FAD + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + ADP + Pi → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4NADH + 4H<sup>+</sup> + FADH<sub>2</sub> + ATP
formula_sheet.note: Includes the link reaction NADH. 15 ATP per pyruvate on the 3/2 rule.

formula_sheet.name: ETS order
formula_sheet.expr: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) → UQ ← Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase); UQ → Complex III (cytochrome bc<sub>1</sub>) → cytochrome c → Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, cyt a, a<sub>3</sub>, 2 Cu centres) → O<sub>2</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>O; Complex V = ATP synthase
formula_sheet.note: Oxygen is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor; it drives the process by removing hydrogen from the system.

formula_sheet.name: ATP per coenzyme and per proton
formula_sheet.expr: 1 NADH → 3 ATP; 1 FADH<sub>2</sub> → 2 ATP; 2H<sup>+</sup> through F<sub>0</sub> per ATP
formula_sheet.note: F<sub>1</sub> headpiece holds the ATP-synthesising site; F<sub>0</sub> forms the proton channel.

formula_sheet.name: Balance sheet
formula_sheet.expr: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (GTP) + 10 NADH × 3 + 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> × 2 = 38; net 36 after 2 ATP to move cytoplasmic NADH into the mitochondrion
formula_sheet.note: Four assumptions: sequential pathway; glycolytic NADH enters mitochondria; no intermediate withdrawn; only glucose respired.

formula_sheet.name: Fermentation vs aerobic
formula_sheet.expr: Partial vs complete oxidation; 2 vs 36 ATP; NADH oxidised slowly by pyruvate/acetaldehyde vs vigorously by O<sub>2</sub> through the ETS
formula_sheet.note: NCERT's three-point comparison at the end of 12.5.

formula_sheet.name: Amphibolic entries
formula_sheet.expr: Fatty acids → acetyl CoA; glycerol → PGAL; amino acids → pyruvate / acetyl CoA / TCA intermediates; withdrawals: acetyl CoA for fatty acids, TCA intermediates for amino acids
formula_sheet.note: NCERT Fig. 12.5. Catabolism and anabolism through the same pathway.

formula_sheet.name: Respiratory quotient
formula_sheet.expr: RQ = volume CO<sub>2</sub> evolved / volume O<sub>2</sub> consumed; carbohydrate 1.0; tripalmitin 102/145 = 0.7; protein about 0.9

formula_sheet.name: Why plants need no breathing organs
formula_sheet.expr: Each part meets its own need; low demand, rates far below animals; O<sub>2</sub> released inside photosynthesising cells; living cells near the surface; large air spaces and dead cells in the bulk
formula_sheet.note: Gas exchange through stomata and lenticels.

diagrams.title: Steps of glycolysis (NCERT Fig. 12.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical flow chart. Glucose at the top; arrow down with 'ATP → ADP, hexokinase' to glucose-6-phosphate; arrow to fructose-6-phosphate; arrow with 'ATP → ADP, phosphofructokinase' to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. Split the arrow (aldolase) into two boxes side by side, dihydroxyacetone phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde, joined by a double-headed arrow (isomerase). From PGAL continue down: '2NAD<sup>+</sup> → 2NADH + 2H<sup>+</sup>' to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; '2ADP → 2ATP' to 3-phosphoglycerate; arrow to 2-phosphoglycerate; 'H<sub>2</sub>O removed, enolase' to phosphoenolpyruvate; '2ADP → 2ATP, pyruvate kinase' to pyruvic acid. Write 'cytoplasm' in a corner and 'net gain: 2 ATP, 2 NADH' at the bottom. Marking points: the two ATP-using steps, the NADH step, the two ATP-forming steps and the split into two 3C molecules.

diagrams.how_to_draw: Glucose at the top with an arrow labelled 'glycolysis (cytoplasm)' down to pyruvic acid in the centre. From pyruvic acid draw three arrows. Left: 'lactate dehydrogenase, NADH + H<sup>+</sup> → NAD<sup>+</sup>' to lactic acid, labelled 'some bacteria, animal muscle'. Middle: 'pyruvic acid decarboxylase, CO<sub>2</sub> released' to acetaldehyde, then 'alcohol dehydrogenase, NADH + H<sup>+</sup> → NAD<sup>+</sup>' to ethanol, labelled 'yeast, anaerobic'. Right: 'pyruvic dehydrogenase, CO<sub>2</sub> released, NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH + H<sup>+</sup>' to acetyl CoA, labelled 'aerobic, mitochondrial matrix', with an arrow onward to the citric acid cycle. Marking points: three products, three enzymes, where CO<sub>2</sub> is released, where NADH is reoxidised.

diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a large circle. At the top, acetyl CoA (2C) entering, meeting oxaloacetic acid (4C) with H<sub>2</sub>O, arrow 'citrate synthase, CoA released' to citric acid (6C). Going clockwise: isocitrate; then arrow with 'CO<sub>2</sub>' out and 'NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH + H<sup>+</sup>' to α-ketoglutaric acid (5C); arrow with 'CO<sub>2</sub>' out, 'NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH + H<sup>+</sup>' and 'CoA in' to succinyl-CoA (4C); arrow with 'GDP + Pi → GTP, CoA out' to succinic acid; arrow with 'FAD → FADH<sub>2</sub>' to fumaric acid; arrow with 'H<sub>2</sub>O' to malic acid; arrow with 'NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH + H<sup>+</sup>' back to oxaloacetic acid. Beside the circle write 'mitochondrial matrix' and the tally per turn: 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, 3 NADH, 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>, 1 GTP. Marking points: correct order of acids, the two CO<sub>2</sub> exits, the three NADH steps, the one FADH<sub>2</sub> step, the GTP step and regeneration of OAA.

diagrams.title: Electron transport system on the inner mitochondrial membrane (NCERT Fig. 12.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal band for the inner membrane with 'intermembrane space' above and 'matrix' below. Embed five blocks left to right: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), Complex III (cytochrome bc<sub>1</sub>), Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, cyt a, a<sub>3</sub>, Cu), Complex V (ATP synthase). Draw UQ as a small mobile circle inside the membrane between I/II and III, and cytochrome c as a small circle on the upper (outer) surface between III and IV. Arrows: NADH + H<sup>+</sup> → NAD<sup>+</sup> at complex I; FADH<sub>2</sub> → FAD at complex II; electron arrows I → UQ, II → UQ, UQ → III → cyt c → IV; from IV, '½O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O' in the matrix. Draw H<sup>+</sup> arrows pumped upward at complexes I, III and IV, and H<sup>+</sup> flowing back down through F<sub>0</sub> of complex V with 'ADP + Pi → ATP' at the F<sub>1</sub> head in the matrix. Marking points: order of complexes, the two mobile carriers, oxygen as final acceptor, the proton gradient and ATP synthase.

diagrams.title: ATP synthase: F<sub>0</sub> and F<sub>1</sub> particles
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a section of the inner membrane. Inside the membrane draw a cylinder labelled F<sub>0</sub> (integral membrane protein complex, proton channel). On the matrix side draw a knob attached by a stalk labelled F<sub>1</sub> (peripheral membrane protein complex, site of ATP synthesis). Show H<sup>+</sup> entering F<sub>0</sub> from the intermembrane space and leaving into the matrix, and write 'ADP + Pi → ATP' beside F<sub>1</sub>. Add the note '2H<sup>+</sup> per ATP'. Marking points: F<sub>0</sub> in membrane as the channel, F<sub>1</sub> projecting into the matrix with the catalytic site, direction of proton flow (intermembrane space to matrix).

diagrams.how_to_draw: Down the centre draw the main line: carbohydrates → glucose → (glycolysis) PGAL → pyruvic acid → acetyl CoA → citric acid cycle → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O with ATP. On the left draw fats → glycerol with an arrow joining at PGAL, and fats → fatty acids with an arrow joining at acetyl CoA. On the right draw proteins → amino acids with three arrows joining at pyruvic acid, at acetyl CoA and at the citric acid cycle (α-ketoglutaric acid, oxaloacetic acid). Make the arrows at acetyl CoA and the cycle double-headed and label them 'withdrawn for synthesis of fatty acids / amino acids'.
