Write 'glycolysis' outside the mitochondrion in the cytoplasm with an arrow carrying pyruvic acid across both membranes into the matrix. In the matrix write 'link reaction (pyruvic acid → acetyl CoA)' and 'citric acid cycle'. Along a crista write 'ETS and oxidative phosphorylation (complexes I to V)'. Marking points: four labelled parts, and the three processes at their correct sites.

diagrams.title: Respiratory balance sheet as a flow chart
diagrams.how_to_draw: Three boxes left to right: Glycolysis (cytoplasm), Link reaction + Citric acid cycle (matrix), ETS (inner membrane). Under box 1 write '2 ATP, 2 NADH'; under box 2 write '2 NADH (link) + 6 NADH + 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> + 2 GTP (two turns)'; draw arrows carrying '10 NADH' and '2 FADH<sub>2</sub>' into box 3 and write '10 × 3 = 30 ATP, 2 × 2 = 4 ATP'. At the bottom write 'Total 2 + 2 + 30 + 4 = 38; less 2 ATP for transporting glycolytic NADH into the mitochondrion = 36 net (NCERT)'. Marking points: substrate-level ATP shown separately from ETS ATP, correct coenzyme counts, the 36/38 explanation.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between (a) Respiration and Combustion (b) Glycolysis and Krebs' cycle (c) Aerobic respiration and Fermentation.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Respiration vs combustion. Respiration is a biochemical oxidation of glucose inside living cells, controlled by enzymes, occurring in many small steps at cell temperature; the energy is released gradually and a part of it is trapped as ATP, and there is no light. Combustion is a physico-chemical oxidation outside cells, needs no enzymes, occurs in a single uncontrolled step at high temperature, and releases all the energy at once as heat and light; none is stored.

(b) Glycolysis vs Krebs' cycle. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix. Glycolysis is a linear pathway of ten steps; the Krebs cycle is cyclic. Glycolysis needs no oxygen and occurs in aerobes and anaerobes; the Krebs cycle occurs only under aerobic conditions. Glycolysis converts one glucose (6C) into two pyruvic acid (3C) with no CO2 released; the Krebs cycle oxidises acetyl CoA completely, releasing two CO2 per turn. Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 (net 2) with 2 NADH; each turn of the Krebs cycle makes 1 GTP, 3 NADH and 1 FADH2.

(c) Aerobic respiration vs fermentation. Aerobic respiration needs oxygen; fermentation does not. Aerobic respiration degrades glucose completely to CO2 and H2O; fermentation breaks it down partially to ethanol and CO2 or lactic acid. Aerobic respiration occurs in cytoplasm and mitochondria; fermentation only in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration gives a net 36 ATP per glucose; fermentation only 2. In aerobic respiration NADH is oxidised vigorously by the ETS with O2 as acceptor; in fermentation NADH is oxidised slowly by pyruvate or acetaldehyde.

ncert_questions.q: What are respiratory substrates? Name the most common respiratory substrate.
ncert_questions.a: Respiratory substrates are the organic compounds that are oxidised in living cells during respiration to release energy. They include carbohydrates, proteins, fats and organic acids. The most common respiratory substrate is glucose. In plants, sucrose is first split by invertase into glucose and fructose, which then enter glycolysis; fats and proteins are used only when carbohydrates are short.

ncert_questions.q: Give the schematic representation of glycolysis.
ncert_questions.a: Draw the NCERT Fig. 12.1 flow chart (see diagrams). Glucose → (hexokinase, ATP → ADP) glucose-6-phosphate → fructose-6-phosphate → (phosphofructokinase, ATP → ADP) fructose 1,6-bisphosphate → (aldolase) dihydroxyacetone phosphate ⇌ 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (2 molecules) → (NAD+ → NADH + H+) 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → (ADP → ATP) 3-phosphoglycerate → 2-phosphoglycerate → (enolase, H2O removed) phosphoenolpyruvate → (pyruvate kinase, ADP → ATP) pyruvic acid. Site: cytoplasm. Net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH + H+, 2 pyruvic acid per glucose. State that ATP is used at two steps (glucose → glucose-6-phosphate; fructose-6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate) and formed at two steps (BPGA → 3-PGA; PEP → pyruvate).

ncert_questions.q: What are the main steps in aerobic respiration? Where does it take place?
ncert_questions.a: Aerobic respiration takes place in the mitochondria (after glycolysis in the cytoplasm). Its main steps are: (i) Glycolysis in the cytoplasm, glucose → 2 pyruvic acid + 2 ATP + 2 NADH. (ii) Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate (link reaction) in the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+, by pyruvic dehydrogenase. (iii) Citric acid (Krebs) cycle in the matrix, acetyl CoA oxidised to 2 CO2 with 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP per turn. (iv) Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where NADH and FADH2 are oxidised, electrons pass through complexes I to IV to oxygen (forming water) and ATP is made by ATP synthase (complex V) through chemiosmosis. Net yield 36 ATP per glucose.

ncert_questions.q: Give the schematic representation of an overall view of Krebs' cycle.
ncert_questions.a: Draw NCERT Fig. 12.3 (see diagrams). Acetyl CoA (2C) + oxaloacetic acid (4C) + H2O → (citrate synthase, CoA released) citric acid (6C) → isocitric acid → (CO2 out, NAD+ → NADH + H+) α-ketoglutaric acid (5C) → (CO2 out, NAD+ → NADH + H+, CoA in) succinyl-CoA (4C) → (GDP + Pi → GTP, CoA out) succinic acid → (FAD → FADH2) fumaric acid → (+ H2O) malic acid → (NAD+ → NADH + H+) oxaloacetic acid. Site: mitochondrial matrix. Per turn: 2 CO2, 3 NADH + H+, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (→ ATP). Overall for one pyruvic acid including the link reaction: Pyruvic acid + 4NAD+ + FAD + 2H2O + ADP + Pi → 3CO2 + 4NADH + 4H+ + FADH2 + ATP.

The electron transport system is the chain of carriers on the inner mitochondrial membrane through which electrons from NADH and FADH2 are passed to oxygen, with the released energy used to make ATP. Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) oxidises NADH from the matrix and passes the electrons to ubiquinone, a mobile carrier in the membrane. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) passes electrons from FADH2, formed at the succinate step of the citric acid cycle, also to ubiquinone. Reduced ubiquinone is oxidised by complex III (cytochrome bc1), which transfers the electrons to cytochrome c, a small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane acting as a mobile carrier between complexes III and IV. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, containing cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres) passes the electrons to molecular oxygen, the final acceptor, which is reduced to water. As electrons flow, protons are pumped into the intermembrane space; they return to the matrix through the F0 channel of ATP synthase (complex V), and the F1 head makes ATP from ADP and Pi (2H+ per ATP). One NADH yields 3 ATP and one FADH2 2 ATP. Because ATP is made using energy from oxidation, the process is oxidative phosphorylation. Oxygen is needed only at the end but drives the whole system by removing hydrogen and regenerating NAD+ and FAD.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between the following: (a) Aerobic respiration and Anaerobic respiration (b) Glycolysis and Fermentation (c) Glycolysis and Citric acid cycle.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Aerobic vs anaerobic respiration. Aerobic needs molecular O2; anaerobic does not. Aerobic gives complete oxidation to CO2 and H2O; anaerobic gives incomplete oxidation to ethanol + CO2 or lactic acid. Aerobic occurs in cytoplasm and mitochondria; anaerobic only in the cytoplasm. Aerobic yields 36 ATP net per glucose; anaerobic only 2. In aerobic respiration the final hydrogen acceptor is O2; in anaerobic it is an organic molecule (pyruvate or acetaldehyde).

(b) Glycolysis vs fermentation. Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose to two pyruvic acid; fermentation is the further anaerobic conversion of pyruvic acid to ethanol + CO2 or lactic acid. Glycolysis produces NADH + H+ and a net 2 ATP; fermentation produces no ATP itself but reoxidises NADH to NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue. Glycolysis is common to aerobic and anaerobic organisms; fermentation occurs only under anaerobic conditions.

(c) Glycolysis vs citric acid cycle. Cytoplasm vs mitochondrial matrix. Linear vs cyclic pathway. No oxygen needed vs needs oxygen indirectly to regenerate NAD+ and FAD. Glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C), no CO2 released vs acetyl CoA → 2 CO2 per turn. Net 2 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose vs 1 GTP + 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 per turn (2 turns per glucose).

ncert_questions.q: What are the assumptions made during the calculation of net gain of ATP?
ncert_questions.a: The net gain of 36 ATP per glucose is a theoretical figure calculated on four assumptions: (i) there is a sequential, orderly pathway functioning, with one substrate forming the next and with glycolysis, TCA cycle and ETS following one after another; (ii) the NADH synthesised in glycolysis is transferred into the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation; (iii) none of the intermediates in the pathway are utilised to synthesise any other compound; (iv) only glucose is being respired, and no other alternative substrates enter the pathway at any intermediary stage. These are not valid in a living system because all pathways work simultaneously and do not take place one after another, substrates enter the pathway and are withdrawn from it as needed, ATP is utilised as and when needed, and enzymatic rates are controlled by many means.

ncert_questions.q: Discuss 'The respiratory pathway is an amphibolic pathway.'
ncert_questions.a: A catabolic pathway breaks molecules down; an anabolic pathway builds them. The respiratory pathway does both, so it is called amphibolic. Catabolic role: besides glucose, other substrates are broken down through it. Fats are split into glycerol and fatty acids; fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle, and glycerol enters glycolysis as PGAL. Proteins are degraded to amino acids, which enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or intermediates of the citric acid cycle after deamination. Anabolic role: the same intermediates are withdrawn for synthesis. When the cell needs fatty acids, acetyl CoA is withdrawn from the pathway; many amino acids are synthesised from intermediates of the citric acid cycle such as α-ketoglutaric acid and oxaloacetic acid; glycerol for fat synthesis comes from PGAL. Since the respiratory pathway is thus involved in both breakdown and synthesis, it is better called an amphibolic pathway than a purely catabolic one (NCERT Fig. 12.5).

ncert_questions.q: Define RQ. What is its value for fats?
ncert_questions.a: The respiratory quotient (RQ) or respiratory ratio is the ratio of the volume of CO2 evolved to the volume of O2 consumed in respiration: RQ = volume of CO2 evolved / volume of O2 consumed. Its value depends on the substrate. For fats RQ is less than 1, about 0.7, because fats are poor in oxygen and need extra O2 for oxidation. For tripalmitin: 2(C51H98O6) + 145O2 → 102CO2 + 98H2O; RQ = 102/145 = 0.7. (For carbohydrates RQ = 1; for proteins about 0.9.)

Oxidative phosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the energy released when the reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2 are oxidised through the electron transport system with oxygen as the final electron acceptor. As electrons pass through complexes I, III and IV on the inner mitochondrial membrane, protons are pumped into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons flow back into the matrix through the F0 channel of ATP synthase (complex V), and this flow drives the F1 headpiece to make ATP; 2H+ pass through F0 per ATP. One NADH gives 3 ATP and one FADH2 gives 2 ATP. It differs from substrate-level phosphorylation, where ATP is made by direct transfer of phosphate from a substrate, and from photophosphorylation, where the energy comes from light.

ncert_questions.q: What is the significance of step-wise release of energy in respiration?
ncert_questions.a: The complete oxidation of glucose releases a large amount of energy (about 686 kcal per mole is often quoted). If it were all released in one step, as in combustion, it would be lost as heat and light and could damage the cell. In respiration the oxidation occurs in a series of small, enzyme-controlled steps, and this has three advantages. (i) A greater fraction of the energy can be trapped in the high-energy bonds of ATP instead of being lost as heat, so the efficiency is higher. (ii) The rate of the pathway can be regulated at each enzyme step according to the cell's needs, so ATP is made as and when required. (iii) The intermediates formed at each step (PGAL, pyruvate, acetyl CoA, α-ketoglutarate, oxaloacetate) can be withdrawn for the synthesis of other biomolecules such as fatty acids and amino acids, which is what makes the pathway amphibolic.

ncert_questions.q: Oxygen is critical for aerobic respiration. Explain its role with respect to ETS.
ncert_questions.a: Oxygen does not take part directly in glycolysis or in the citric acid cycle; its role is limited to the terminal stage of the ETS. Yet its presence is vital because it is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor: complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) transfers the electrons carried down the chain to molecular O2, which combines with protons to form water. By accepting the electrons, oxygen keeps the whole chain flowing, which keeps the proton gradient and ATP synthesis going, and regenerates NAD+ and FAD from NADH and FADH2. Without oxygen the carriers stay reduced, NAD+ and FAD are not regenerated, the citric acid cycle and the link reaction stop, and the cell is left with only glycolysis and fermentation. NCERT sums it up: oxygen drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the anaerobic respiration or fermentation much less efficient than aerobic respiration in terms of energy yield?
ncert_questions.a: In fermentation glucose is only partially oxidised: the products, ethanol or lactic acid, still hold most of the energy of glucose. The NADH + H+ formed in glycolysis is not oxidised through the ETS but is used to reduce pyruvate or acetaldehyde, so no ATP is made from it. There is no citric acid cycle, no ETS and no oxidative phosphorylation, which is where most of the ATP of aerobic respiration comes from. The only ATP is the net 2 ATP of glycolysis, and less than 7 per cent of the energy in glucose is released, not all of it trapped in ATP. In aerobic respiration glucose is completely oxidised to CO2 and H2O and the reduced coenzymes are oxidised by oxygen through the ETS, giving a net 36 ATP per glucose.

pyq.q: Which biomolecule is common to the respiration-mediated breakdown of fats, carbohydrates and proteins?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, glucose reaches it through pyruvate, and several amino acids are converted to it; pyruvic acid is not formed from fatty acids. Asked in NEET 2013 and 2016.

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about the Krebs cycle is incorrect?
options: There are three points in the cycle where NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH + H<sup>+</sup>
The cycle starts with condensation of the acetyl group with pyruvic acid
GTP is synthesised during the conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinic acid
There is one point where FAD is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The cycle starts with condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid, not pyruvic acid. The other three statements are correct. Asked in NEET 2017.

pyq.q: The energy-releasing metabolic process in which a substrate is oxidised without an external electron acceptor is called
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In fermentation the electron acceptor is an internal organic molecule (pyruvate or acetaldehyde), not external oxygen. Glycolysis alone is not a complete energy-releasing process without the NADH being reoxidised.

pyq.q: The chemiosmotic coupling hypothesis of oxidative phosphorylation proposes that ATP is formed because
options: ADP is pumped out of the matrix into the intermembrane space
High-energy bonds are formed in mitochondrial proteins
A proton gradient forms across the inner mitochondrial membrane
The inner membrane becomes permeable to ADP
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Electron flow pumps protons into the intermembrane space; their return through F<sub>0</sub> of ATP synthase drives ATP synthesis at F<sub>1</sub>.

pyq.q: The electron transport system in a eukaryotic cell is located in the
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Complexes I to V are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane; the citric acid cycle is in the matrix.

pyq.q: During which stage of aerobic respiration is the greatest number of ATP molecules formed from ADP?
options: Conversion of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The ETS oxidises 10 NADH and 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> to give 34 ATP; glycolysis and the Krebs cycle give only 2 ATP each by substrate-level phosphorylation, and the link reaction gives none directly.

pyq.q: In alcoholic fermentation
options: Triose phosphate is the electron donor while acetaldehyde is the electron acceptor
Triose phosphate is the electron donor while pyruvic acid is the electron acceptor
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NADH is formed when PGAL (a triose phosphate) is oxidised in glycolysis and is reoxidised when acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase. Pyruvate is the acceptor in lactic acid fermentation, not alcoholic.

pyq.q: Pyruvic acid, the key product of glycolysis, can have many metabolic fates. Under aerobic conditions it forms
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In the mitochondrial matrix pyruvic acid undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase to acetyl CoA, CO<sub>2</sub> and NADH; CO<sub>2</sub> and water are the end products only after the citric acid cycle and ETS.

pyq.q: The respiratory quotient of tripalmitin is about
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: 2(C<sub>51</sub>H<sub>98</sub>O<sub>6</sub>) + 145O<sub>2</sub> → 102CO<sub>2</sub> + 98H<sub>2</sub>O; RQ = 102/145 = 0.7. Carbohydrates give 1.0 and proteins about 0.9.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Fermentation releases much less energy than aerobic respiration. Reason (R): In fermentation glucose is only partially oxidised and the NADH of glycolysis is used to reduce pyruvate or acetaldehyde instead of being oxidised through the ETS.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both are NCERT statements and R gives exactly why only 2 ATP are made and less than 7 per cent of the energy of glucose is released.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms. Reason (R): Glycolysis requires molecular oxygen for the oxidation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Glycolysis is universal and needs no oxygen; the oxidation of PGAL is done by NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH + H<sup>+</sup>.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Oxygen is essential for aerobic respiration even though it does not take part directly in the citric acid cycle. Reason (R): Oxygen is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor at the end of the ETS, and by removing hydrogen it regenerates NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD needed by the cycle.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT: the role of oxygen is limited to the terminal stage, but its presence is vital since it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): ATP synthase is called complex V of the electron transport system. Reason (R): ATP synthase transfers electrons from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: ATP synthase is complex V, but it carries no electrons; electrons are handed to oxygen by complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase. Complex V only conducts protons through F<sub>0</sub> and makes ATP at F<sub>1</sub>.

pyq.q: Define respiratory quotient. Why is the RQ of fats less than one?
pyq.answer:
RQ is the ratio of the volume of CO2 evolved to the volume of O2 consumed in respiration: RQ = volume CO2 evolved / volume O2 consumed. (1 mark)

Fats contain much less oxygen in proportion to carbon and hydrogen than carbohydrates do, so more O2 has to be taken in to oxidise them fully, and less CO2 is released per O2 consumed. For tripalmitin, 145 O2 are consumed and 102 CO2 released, RQ = 0.7. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is substrate-level phosphorylation? Give one example each from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle.
pyq.answer:
Substrate-level phosphorylation is the formation of ATP (or GTP) by the direct transfer of a phosphate group from a phosphorylated substrate to ADP (or GDP), without an electron transport chain or proton gradient. (1 mark)

Glycolysis: conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate, or of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvic acid, each forming ATP. Citric acid cycle: conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinic acid, forming GTP, which then gives ATP. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Name the two parts of ATP synthase and state the function of each.
pyq.answer:
F1: the headpiece, a peripheral membrane protein complex projecting into the matrix, which contains the site for synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. (1 mark)

F0: an integral membrane protein complex that forms the channel through which protons cross the inner membrane from the intermembrane space to the matrix; the passage of 2H+ through it is coupled to the synthesis of one ATP at F1. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Plants do not have specialised organs for gas exchange. Give two reasons why they can manage without them.
pyq.answer: (i) Each plant part takes care of its own gas-exchange needs through stomata and lenticels, and plants do not present a great demand for gas exchange since roots, stems and leaves respire at rates far lower than animals. (ii) Living cells lie close to the surface of the plant, and the bulk of the body is dead cells or loosely packed parenchyma with large intercellular spaces, so gases diffuse easily; in addition, photosynthesising cells release O2 within the cell. (1 mark each for any two)

pyq.q: What is oxidative decarboxylation? Name the enzyme and the coenzymes involved when pyruvate undergoes it.
pyq.answer:
Oxidative decarboxylation is a reaction in which a molecule loses CO2 and is simultaneously oxidised, the hydrogen being taken up by a coenzyme. Pyruvic acid (3C) is converted in the mitochondrial matrix to acetyl CoA (2C) + CO2 + NADH + H+. (1 mark)

Enzyme: pyruvic dehydrogenase (needs Mg2+). Coenzymes: NAD+ and coenzyme A. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Describe alcoholic fermentation in yeast. Why can naturally fermented drinks not exceed about 13 per cent alcohol?
pyq.answer:
Under anaerobic conditions yeast converts the pyruvic acid formed in glycolysis into ethanol and CO2 in two steps. First, pyruvic acid is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde by pyruvic acid decarboxylase, releasing CO2. Then acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase, with NADH + H+ being oxidised to NAD+; this regeneration of NAD+ allows glycolysis to continue. Overall: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2, with a net gain of only 2 ATP from glycolysis; less than 7 per cent of the energy of glucose is released. (2 marks)

Ethanol is toxic to the yeast itself. As fermentation proceeds the alcohol accumulates, and yeasts poison themselves to death when the concentration reaches about 13 per cent, so fermentation stops; stronger drinks are made by distillation. (1 mark)

pyq.q: State the assumptions on which the net gain of ATP in aerobic respiration is calculated, and say why they do not hold in a living cell.
pyq.answer:
Assumptions: (i) a sequential, orderly pathway with one substrate forming the next and glycolysis, TCA cycle and ETS following one after another; (ii) the NADH made in glycolysis is transferred into the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation; (iii) none of the intermediates is used to synthesise any other compound; (iv) only glucose is respired, with no other substrate entering at an intermediate stage. (2 marks)

In a living cell all pathways work simultaneously rather than one after another, substrates enter and leave the pathway at many points (the pathway is amphibolic), ATP is used as and when needed, and enzyme rates are regulated, so the actual yield varies; the figure of 36 ATP is theoretical. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Explain the chemiosmotic mechanism of ATP synthesis in mitochondria.
pyq.answer:
As electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass through complexes I, III and IV of the ETS on the inner mitochondrial membrane, the energy released is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. This creates a proton (electrochemical) gradient across the inner membrane, which is impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase. (1 mark)

ATP synthase (complex V) has F0, an integral membrane protein complex forming a proton channel, and F1, a peripheral headpiece in the matrix containing the catalytic site. Protons flow back into the matrix through F0 down the gradient, and this flow is coupled to the synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi at F1; for each ATP, 2H+ pass through F0. (1 mark)

Since the energy comes from the oxidation of coenzymes with oxygen as the final acceptor, the process is called oxidative phosphorylation; one NADH yields 3 ATP and one FADH2 yields 2 ATP. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Give three differences between glycolysis and the citric acid cycle.
pyq.answer: (i) Site: glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix. (ii) Oxygen: glycolysis needs no oxygen and occurs in all organisms; the citric acid cycle runs only under aerobic conditions because NAD+ and FAD are regenerated by the ETS. (iii) Pathway and products: glycolysis is linear, converting one glucose (6C) into two pyruvic acid (3C) with a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH and no CO2; the citric acid cycle is cyclic, oxidising acetyl CoA to two CO2 per turn with 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP, and regenerating oxaloacetic acid. (1 mark each)

pyq.q: Write the three possible fates of pyruvic acid formed in glycolysis, naming the enzyme and the condition for each.
pyq.answer: (i) Lactic acid fermentation: under anaerobic conditions in some bacteria and in animal muscle short of oxygen, pyruvic acid is reduced by NADH + H+ to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase; no CO2 is released. (ii) Alcoholic fermentation: under anaerobic conditions in yeast, pyruvic acid is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase, releasing CO2. (iii) Aerobic respiration: in the presence of oxygen pyruvic acid enters the mitochondrial matrix and undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase (with NAD+ and CoA) to acetyl CoA, CO2 and NADH + H+; acetyl CoA then enters the citric acid cycle. (1 mark each)

pyq.q: Describe glycolysis with a schematic representation. Indicate the steps at which ATP is used and formed and state the net gain per glucose.
pyq.answer:
Glycolysis (EMP pathway, after Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas) is the partial oxidation of glucose to two molecules of pyruvic acid in the cytoplasm; it needs no oxygen and occurs in all living organisms. (1 mark)

Scheme (draw NCERT Fig. 12.1): Glucose → (hexokinase, ATP used) glucose-6-phosphate → fructose-6-phosphate → (phosphofructokinase, ATP used) fructose 1,6-bisphosphate → (aldolase) dihydroxyacetone phosphate + 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (DHAP isomerises to PGAL, so two PGAL per glucose) → (NAD+ → NADH + H+) 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → (ATP formed) 3-phosphoglycerate → 2-phosphoglycerate → (enolase, H2O removed) phosphoenolpyruvate → (pyruvate kinase, ATP formed) pyruvic acid. (2 marks)

ATP used: at the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate and of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (2 ATP). ATP formed: at the conversion of BPGA to 3-PGA and of PEP to pyruvic acid, by substrate-level phosphorylation; each occurs twice per glucose (4 ATP). NADH: formed when PGAL is oxidised to BPGA, twice per glucose. (1 mark)

Net gain per glucose: 2 ATP (4 formed minus 2 used), 2 NADH + H+ and 2 pyruvic acid. Pyruvic acid then goes to lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation or aerobic respiration depending on the organism and on oxygen. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Describe the citric acid cycle with a labelled schematic. Give its overall equation for one molecule of pyruvic acid and the tally of products per turn.
pyq.answer:
The tricarboxylic acid (citric acid or Krebs) cycle was elucidated by Hans Krebs in 1937 and occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvic acid first undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase to acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+. (1 mark)

Cycle (draw NCERT Fig. 12.3): Acetyl CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetic acid (4C) and water to give citric acid (6C), catalysed by citrate synthase; CoA is released. Citrate is isomerised to isocitrate. Isocitrate loses CO2 and is oxidised (NAD+ → NADH + H+) to α-ketoglutaric acid (5C). α-Ketoglutaric acid loses a second CO2, is oxidised (second NADH + H+) and combines with CoA to form succinyl-CoA (4C). Succinyl-CoA is converted to succinic acid with the synthesis of GTP from GDP + Pi (substrate-level phosphorylation); GTP then forms ATP from ADP. Succinic acid is oxidised by succinate dehydrogenase to fumaric acid, with FAD reduced to FADH2. Fumaric acid adds water to form malic acid, which is oxidised (third NADH + H+) to oxaloacetic acid, regenerating the acceptor. (2 marks)

Per turn: 2 CO2, 3 NADH + H+, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (= 1 ATP); two turns per glucose. (1 mark)

Overall equation for one pyruvic acid (with the link reaction): Pyruvic acid + 4NAD+ + FAD + 2H2O + ADP + Pi → 3CO2 + 4NADH + 4H+ + FADH2 + ATP. The continued oxidation of acetyl CoA requires continued replenishment of oxaloacetic acid and regeneration of NAD+ and FAD by the ETS. (1 mark)

pyq.q: With a labelled diagram, describe the electron transport system of mitochondria and explain how ATP is synthesised. What is the role of oxygen?
pyq.answer:
The ETS is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane (draw NCERT Fig. 12.4 with the membrane, intermembrane space above, matrix below, and complexes I to V). (1 mark for the diagram)

Carriers: NADH from the matrix is oxidised by complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), which passes the electrons to ubiquinone, a mobile carrier within the membrane. Ubiquinone also receives electrons from FADH2 through complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). Reduced ubiquinone is oxidised by complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex), which transfers the electrons to cytochrome c, a small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane that shuttles between complexes III and IV. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), containing cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres, transfers the electrons to molecular oxygen, which is reduced to water. (2 marks)

ATP synthesis: as electrons pass through the complexes, protons are pumped into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons return to the matrix through the F0 channel of ATP synthase (complex V), and the F1 headpiece uses this flow to make ATP from ADP and Pi; 2H+ pass per ATP. One NADH gives 3 ATP, one FADH2 gives 2 ATP, because FADH2 enters after complex I. This is oxidative phosphorylation. (1 mark)

Role of oxygen: oxygen acts only at the terminal step, as the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor, but its presence is vital because it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system, regenerating NAD+ and FAD and keeping the citric acid cycle and the proton pumping going. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Prepare the respiratory balance sheet for the complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose, showing the ATP obtained at each stage. Why does NCERT give the net gain as 36 ATP?
pyq.answer:
Assume 3 ATP per NADH and 2 ATP per FADH2 oxidised in the ETS, and the four NCERT assumptions (sequential pathway, glycolytic NADH enters the mitochondrion, no intermediate withdrawn, only glucose respired). (1 mark)

  • Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation (4 formed, 2 used) + 2 NADH + H+.
  • Oxidative decarboxylation of 2 pyruvate (matrix): 2 NADH + H+.
  • Citric acid cycle, 2 turns (matrix): 2 GTP = 2 ATP + 6 NADH + H+ + 2 FADH2.
  • ETS (inner membrane): 10 NADH × 3 = 30 ATP; 2 FADH2 × 2 = 4 ATP.

(2 marks for the stage-wise tally)

Total: 2 + 2 + 30 + 4 = 38 ATP. (1 mark)

The 2 NADH of glycolysis are made in the cytoplasm and must be transported across the mitochondrial membranes to reach the ETS; this transport costs the equivalent of 2 ATP, so the net gain is 38 − 2 = 36 ATP per glucose, the figure NCERT gives. In fermentation, by contrast, the net gain is only 2 ATP. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
A student sets up three respirometers with germinating seeds. Flask A holds germinating wheat grains, flask B holds germinating castor seeds, and flask C holds germinating wheat grains but is sealed so that no oxygen can enter. After some hours the student measures the CO2 released and the O2 consumed. Flask A shows the two volumes almost equal; flask B shows less CO2 released than O2 consumed; flask C shows CO2 released although no O2 was consumed.
(i) Define the quantity the student is measuring.
(ii) State the approximate RQ in flasks A and B and name the substrate being respired in each.
(iii) Explain the observation in flask C and name the process going on in the seeds.
(iv) Why would a value near 0.9 be expected from seeds respiring mainly proteins?
pyq.answer:
(i) The respiratory quotient, the ratio of the volume of CO2 evolved to the volume of O2 consumed in respiration. (1 mark)

(ii) Flask A: RQ about 1, the wheat grains are respiring carbohydrate (starch → glucose), C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O. Flask B: RQ below 1, about 0.7, the castor seeds are respiring fat (oil), which is poor in oxygen and needs more O2 per CO2 released, as for tripalmitin, 102/145 = 0.7. (1 mark)

(iii) Without oxygen the seeds carry out fermentation (anaerobic respiration): glycolysis gives pyruvic acid, which is converted to ethanol and CO2 by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase, so CO2 is released although no O2 is consumed; the RQ cannot be defined meaningfully (it tends to infinity). (1 mark)

(iv) Proteins contain more oxygen relative to carbon than fats but less than carbohydrates, so their RQ lies between the two; NCERT gives about 0.9 for proteins as the respiratory substrate. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
In a bakery, yeast is mixed into dough and left in a warm place. The dough rises and smells faintly of alcohol. The same baker makes wine from grape juice with the same yeast, but finds that the alcohol content never rises beyond about 13 per cent no matter how long the juice is kept, and that the yeast in the wine is dead by the end.
(i) Name the process occurring in the dough and write its overall equation.
(ii) Name the two enzymes involved and the coenzyme that is recycled.
(iii) Why does the alcohol content stop at about 13 per cent?
(iv) How much of the energy of glucose is released in this process, and how many ATP does the yeast gain per glucose?
pyq.answer:
(i) Alcoholic fermentation, an anaerobic process in yeast: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy; the CO2 makes the dough rise. (1 mark)

(ii) Pyruvic acid decarboxylase converts pyruvic acid to acetaldehyde and CO2; alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol. The coenzyme NADH + H+ formed in glycolysis is oxidised back to NAD+, which is recycled so that glycolysis can continue. (1 mark)

(iii) Ethanol is toxic to yeast. Yeasts poison themselves to death when the alcohol concentration reaches about 13 per cent, so fermentation stops at that level; stronger spirits are obtained only by distillation. (1 mark)

(iv) Less than 7 per cent of the energy in glucose is released in fermentation, and not all of it is trapped in ATP; the net gain is only the 2 ATP of glycolysis per glucose, compared with 36 in aerobic respiration. (1 mark)

practice_mcq.q: Glycolysis takes place in the
practice_mcq.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of all living cells and needs no oxygen; only the later stages of aerobic respiration are in the mitochondrion.

practice_mcq.q: The scheme of glycolysis was given by
practice_mcq.explanation: Glycolysis is also called the EMP pathway after Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas; Krebs elucidated the citric acid cycle.

practice_mcq.q: In which step of glycolysis is NAD<sup>+</sup> reduced to NADH + H<sup>+</sup>?
practice_mcq.explanation: PGAL is oxidised and phosphorylated to BPGA, and the two hydrogens removed are transferred to NAD<sup>+</sup>; this is the only NADH step of glycolysis.

practice_mcq.q: The net gain of ATP and NADH per molecule of glucose in glycolysis is
practice_mcq.explanation: Four ATP are formed by substrate-level phosphorylation and two are used in the first phase, giving a net 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH + H<sup>+</sup>.

practice_mcq.q: The enzyme that converts sucrose into glucose and fructose before glycolysis in plants is
practice_mcq.explanation: Invertase splits sucrose; hexokinase then phosphorylates glucose. Aldolase and enolase act later in glycolysis.

practice_mcq.q: Which enzyme catalyses the reduction of pyruvic acid to lactic acid in muscle cells short of oxygen?
practice_mcq.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate using NADH + H<sup>+</sup>. The first two belong to alcoholic fermentation and the last to the aerobic link reaction.

practice_mcq.q: Yeasts poison themselves to death when the alcohol concentration reaches about
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states about 13 per cent; this is why naturally fermented beverages are not stronger, and spirits need distillation.

practice_mcq.q: In fermentation, what fraction of the energy in glucose is released?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose is released in fermentation, and not all of it is trapped as ATP.

practice_mcq.q: The oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA is catalysed by
practice_mcq.explanation: Pyruvic dehydrogenase, with NAD<sup>+</sup> and CoA as coenzymes and Mg<sup>2+</sup>, converts pyruvate to acetyl CoA in the matrix; pyruvic acid decarboxylase (no oxidation) acts in yeast fermentation.

practice_mcq.q: In the citric acid cycle, GTP is formed during the conversion of
practice_mcq.explanation: The thioester bond of succinyl-CoA powers the only substrate-level phosphorylation of the cycle, forming GTP that is then converted to ATP.

practice_mcq.q: FADH<sub>2</sub> is produced in the citric acid cycle at the step
practice_mcq.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD as acceptor; the isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate and malate oxidations use NAD<sup>+</sup>, and fumarate → malate is a hydration.

practice_mcq.q: How many molecules of NADH + H<sup>+</sup> and FADH<sub>2</sub> are formed per turn of the citric acid cycle?
practice_mcq.explanation: Three NAD<sup>+</sup> reductions (isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, malate) and one FAD reduction (succinate) per acetyl CoA. Four NADH applies per pyruvate if the link reaction is included.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a mobile carrier of electrons between complex III and complex IV?
practice_mcq.explanation: Cytochrome c is a small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane that shuttles electrons from the cytochrome bc<sub>1</sub> complex to cytochrome c oxidase. Ubiquinone is mobile between complexes I/II and III.

practice_mcq.q: Complex IV of the mitochondrial ETS contains
options: Cytochromes a and a<sub>3</sub> with two copper centres
practice_mcq.explanation: Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, which contains cytochromes a and a<sub>3</sub> and two copper centres and passes electrons to oxygen. F<sub>0</sub>-F<sub>1</sub> is complex V.

practice_mcq.q: The number of ATP molecules formed from the oxidation of one FADH<sub>2</sub> in the ETS is
practice_mcq.explanation: FADH<sub>2</sub> donates electrons to ubiquinone via complex II, bypassing complex I, so it yields 2 ATP against 3 for NADH.

practice_mcq.q: For each ATP produced by ATP synthase, the number of protons that pass through F<sub>0</sub> from the intermembrane space to the matrix is
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: for each ATP produced, 2H<sup>+</sup> pass through F<sub>0</sub> down the electrochemical proton gradient.

practice_mcq.q: If the complete oxidation of one mole of glucose yields 686 kcal and one high-energy ATP bond is taken as 12 kcal, the maximum number of ATP that could theoretically be generated per glucose is about
practice_mcq.explanation: 686 ÷ 12 = 57.2, so about 57 if all the energy were trapped. The cell actually makes 36 to 38, which shows why a fraction is lost as heat.

practice_mcq.q: According to NCERT, the net gain of ATP during aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose is
practice_mcq.explanation: 38 are formed on the 3-per-NADH, 2-per-FADH<sub>2</sub> rule, but 2 are spent moving the glycolytic NADH into the mitochondrion, so NCERT gives a net gain of 36.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is not one of the assumptions made in calculating the net gain of ATP?
options: Glycolysis, TCA cycle and ETS follow one after another
The NADH of glycolysis enters the mitochondrion and is oxidised there
Intermediates are withdrawn for the synthesis of other compounds
practice_mcq.explanation: The assumption is the opposite: none of the intermediates is used to synthesise any other compound. Withdrawal of intermediates is what happens in real cells.

practice_mcq.q: Glycerol obtained from the breakdown of fats enters the respiratory pathway as
practice_mcq.explanation: Glycerol is converted to PGAL and enters glycolysis; fatty acids, not glycerol, are broken to acetyl CoA.

practice_mcq.q: The respiratory quotient when carbohydrates are the respiratory substrate is
practice_mcq.explanation: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> → 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O gives 6/6 = 1.0; fats give about 0.7 and proteins about 0.9.

practice_mcq.q: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is
practice_mcq.explanation: Complex IV hands the electrons to molecular oxygen, which is reduced to water; cytochrome c and ubiquinone are intermediate carriers.

common_mistakes: Writing NADPH for the coenzyme reduced in glycolysis or the citric acid cycle. Respiration uses NAD<sup>+</sup>/NADH and FAD/FADH<sub>2</sub>; NADPH belongs to photosynthesis. Examiners cut the mark for the wrong coenzyme even when the step is right.

Saying that pyruvic acid enters the Krebs cycle. Pyruvic acid is first converted to acetyl CoA in the matrix, and it is acetyl CoA that condenses with oxaloacetic acid. NEET 2017 built a whole question on this.

Placing FADH<sub>2</sub> at the wrong step or GTP at the wrong step. FADH<sub>2</sub> is made only at succinate → fumarate; GTP only at succinyl-CoA → succinate. Students who draw the cycle from memory often swap these.

Giving 38 ATP as the NCERT answer. NCERT gives a net gain of 36 ATP, with the 2 ATP difference being the cost of moving glycolytic NADH into the mitochondrion. Write 36 and be able to show 38 minus 2.

Confusing the sites. Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm, not the mitochondrion; the citric acid cycle is in the matrix, not the inner membrane; the ETS is on the inner membrane, not in the matrix. A 1-mark site question is lost by a single wrong word.

Calling oxygen a participant in the Krebs cycle. Oxygen is used only at the end of the ETS as the final hydrogen acceptor; the cycle needs it indirectly, to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD. Say this exactly.

Defining RQ as amount or moles instead of volume, or inverting it. RQ is the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> evolved divided by the volume of O<sub>2</sub> consumed; tripalmitin gives 102/145 = 0.7, not 145/102.

Writing fermentation as 'respiration without oxygen' and stopping there. The examiner wants the enzymes (pyruvic acid decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase, lactate dehydrogenase), the reoxidation of NADH to NAD<sup>+</sup>, the 2 ATP and the less-than-7-per-cent figure.

Mixing up F<sub>0</sub> and F<sub>1</sub>. F<sub>1</sub> is the headpiece in the matrix with the ATP-synthesising site; F<sub>0</sub> is the membrane-embedded proton channel. And ATP synthase carries protons, not electrons.

Answering the amphibolic question with a definition only. The mark is for one catabolic example and one anabolic example with named molecules: fatty acids to acetyl CoA, and acetyl CoA withdrawn for fatty-acid synthesis.
strategy:
This chapter is one pathway told in order, so prepare it in order and do not skip the counts. Spend the first sitting on glycolysis: draw Fig. 12.1 three times from memory until you can mark the two ATP-using steps, the NADH step and the two ATP-forming steps without looking, and write the net gain at the bottom each time. Spend the second sitting on the fates of pyruvate (Fig. 12.2) and the citric acid cycle (Fig. 12.3); for the cycle learn the order of the acids as a chant (citrate, isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate, oxaloacetate) and pin the three events to their steps: GTP at succinyl-CoA, FADH2 at succinate, NADH at isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate and malate.

The third sitting is the ETS (Fig. 12.4): five complexes in order, ubiquinone and cytochrome c as the two mobile carriers, oxygen at the end, F0 and F1 with 2H+ per ATP, 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2. Then do the balance sheet once on paper and reach 38 and then 36; the four assumptions are a guaranteed 2 or 3 marks, so memorise them as four short lines.

The last sitting is the small sections that give cheap marks: why plants need no breathing organs (five reasons), the amphibolic pathway with two examples each way, and RQ with the tripalmitin arithmetic. Finish by writing the NCERT exercise 12.1 and 12.7 comparison tables; they are the most likely 5-mark question in a school paper. In the exam, give every biochemical answer as a labelled scheme plus a tally line; the tally (ATP, NADH, FADH2, CO2) is where the marks sit.
revision_checklist: Overall equation of aerobic respiration and the two differences from combustion (enzyme-controlled, step-wise; energy trapped as ATP).
Five reasons plants need no specialised breathing organs; gas exchange through stomata and lenticels.
Glycolysis: cytoplasm, EMP, ten steps in order, ATP used at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase steps, ATP formed at BPGA → 3-PGA and PEP → pyruvate, NADH at PGAL → BPGA, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
Three fates of pyruvic acid with enzyme and condition for each; Fig. 12.2.
Fermentation: less than 7 per cent of energy released, 2 ATP, yeast dies at about 13 per cent alcohol, NADH reoxidised to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Link reaction: pyruvic dehydrogenase, NAD<sup>+</sup> and CoA, matrix, acetyl CoA + CO<sub>2</sub> + NADH.
Citric acid cycle: order of acids, GTP at succinyl-CoA → succinate, FADH<sub>2</sub> at succinate → fumarate, 3 NADH per turn, 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, Hans Krebs 1937, matrix.
NCERT summary equation per pyruvate: 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4NADH + 4H<sup>+</sup> + FADH<sub>2</sub> + ATP.
ETS order: complex I, II → UQ → III → cyt c → IV → O<sub>2</sub>; complex IV has cyt a, a<sub>3</sub> and two Cu centres; complex V is ATP synthase.
F<sub>1</sub> headpiece (ATP site) and F<sub>0</sub> channel; 2H<sup>+</sup> per ATP; 3 ATP per NADH, 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>; oxidative phosphorylation defined.
Role of oxygen: final hydrogen acceptor, drives the process by removing hydrogen, regenerates NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD.
Balance sheet: four assumptions; 2 + 2 + 30 + 4 = 38; net 36 after transport of glycolytic NADH.
Fermentation versus aerobic respiration: partial versus complete oxidation, 2 versus 36 ATP, slow versus vigorous NADH oxidation.
Amphibolic pathway: fatty acids → acetyl CoA, glycerol → PGAL, amino acids → pyruvate/acetyl CoA/TCA intermediates; withdrawals for fatty acid and amino acid synthesis.
RQ = volume CO<sub>2</sub> / volume O<sub>2</sub>; carbohydrate 1.0, tripalmitin 102/145 = 0.7, protein about 0.9.
